"Noor, you're up at five again for that class?"
"It's my course, Abba. I'm going."
Thomas put down his tea. "Last week you said you hate it."
"I don't hate it. I just don't like any of it."
"That sounds like hate."
"We've paid for six months already. You paid."
"I'm not asking for the money back. I'm asking if you're happy."
"I told everyone I'm doing animation. Rizwana even put it in the group."
"So?"
"So if I quit, I'm the girl who couldn't finish anything."
"Or the girl who found something out."
Noor pulled on her jacket. "Three more months. I started it, I'll finish it."
The door closed. Thomas sat looking at his cold tea.

qa.q: How many months had already been paid for?
qa.a: Six months.

qa.q: Why does Noor insist "I started it, I'll finish it" even though she dislikes the course?
qa.a: She fears quitting would make her "the girl who couldn't finish anything", especially after telling everyone; staying consistent feels safer than admitting the choice was wrong.

qa.q: What turning point did Thomas offer that Noor could take up later?
qa.a: He said he wasn't asking for the money back, only whether she is happy; that removes the "wasted fees" reason and invites her to judge the course by how it feels now.

qa.q: What might Thomas be feeling as he looks at his cold tea?
qa.a: He may feel worried and a bit helpless, watching his daughter force herself through something she dislikes because of what others will think. 😔

grounding: A young woman keeps attending a course she dislikes because fees are paid and friends were told, and quitting feels like admitting a mistake.

passage: Looking back, the worst months were the ones I spent pretending. I'm Yamini, and last year I signed up for a paid accountancy foundation course because it "sounded secure." By the third month, I dreaded every class. But I had already paid two instalments, and I'd told everyone at my cousin's wedding. So I kept going, highlighting pages I didn't understand, feeling a little flatter each evening. When Vaibhav asked if I liked it, I snapped, "I'm not a quitter." The truth is, I wasn't choosing the course anymore. I was choosing not to look like I'd made a mistake. I still attend. I'm still not sure what to do about it.

qa.q: How many instalments had Yamini already paid?
qa.a: Two instalments.

qa.q: Why did Yamini snap "I'm not a quitter" at Vaibhav?
qa.a: Vaibhav's question touched the doubt Yamini was hiding; after the fees and the wedding announcement, quitting felt like admitting a mistake.

qa.q: What question could help Yamini separate the past choice from the present one?
qa.a: Whether, knowing what Yamini knows now, the course would be chosen today; the instalments already paid stay paid either way.

qa.q: How might Vaibhav feel after being snapped at?
qa.a: Vaibhav asked a simple, caring question and got a sharp answer, so Vaibhav may feel hurt or unsure whether to raise it again.

grounding: A young adult keeps attending a disliked course because fees are paid and people were told, and quitting feels like admitting an error.

Counsellor's note — Gopika, student wellness centre
Sangeeta, 19, came in about poor sleep. She is in the second year of a paid diploma in hotel management and says she has "no interest at all" in it. Her face lit up when she talked about the gardening club, then dropped when I asked about the diploma. When I asked why she continues, she listed: fees already paid by her uncle, a year already spent, and "everyone at home knows." She said leaving would mean admitting she chose wrong. She didn't mention liking any part of it. Next step: I've offered a second session to look at what she would choose if starting fresh, and to plan how she could talk honestly with her uncle.

qa.q: What made Sangeeta's face light up?
qa.a: Talking about the gardening club.

qa.q: What does Sangeeta mean when she says leaving would be admitting she chose wrong?
qa.a: She fears quitting would show her first decision was a mistake, so staying consistent feels safer, even though she doesn't like any part of the diploma.

qa.q: What next step did Gopika offer, and why could it help?
qa.a: A second session on what Sangeeta would choose if starting fresh, and how to talk honestly with her uncle, so the choice rests on the present, not on fees and a year spent.

qa.q: How might Sangeeta's uncle be affected if she keeps quiet?
qa.a: He may keep paying for a diploma she has no interest in without knowing the truth, and could later feel hurt that she didn't tell him sooner.

grounding: A counsellor notes a young woman staying in a disliked, paid diploma because of fees, time spent and family knowing, since leaving feels like admitting error.

passage:
Thursday, 11:40 p.m.
Coding bootcamp, week fourteen. Today's project was a login page. I sat there for three hours and felt nothing except a dull headache.
Nirmala Bua paid half the fees. I paid the other half from my savings from the bakery job. Six months, gone into this. And at my farewell from the bakery I told everyone, 'I'm going to be a developer.' They clapped. Uncle Baljinder even gave me a keyboard.
So I can't quit now. What would I say? 'Sorry, I was wrong'? Everyone would look at me like that.
The only good part of my day was lunch, when I helped the canteen aunty ice a cake for someone's birthday. My hands knew what to do. I didn't want to go back to the laptop.
I'm annoyed with myself, with the course, with everyone who clapped.
Eight more weeks. I'll finish. I have to.
Gurpreet

qa.q: Who paid half of Gurpreet's bootcamp fees?
qa.a: Nirmala Bua paid half the fees.

qa.q: What does Gurpreet feel about the course and the people who clapped?
qa.a: Gurpreet feels resentful and annoyed with the course, with Gurpreet's own choice and with everyone who clapped, but trapped because quitting feels like admitting being wrong.

qa.q: What small step could Gurpreet take before the next eight weeks?
qa.a: Gurpreet could talk honestly with Nirmala Bua about how the course feels and about enjoying the cake work, instead of pushing on only because of fees and the farewell.

qa.q: How might Nirmala Bua feel if she read this diary?
qa.a: Nirmala Bua would probably be worried and would likely care more about Gurpreet's happiness than about the fees already paid.

grounding: A young adult keeps attending a disliked bootcamp because of fees spent and a public announcement, feeling resentful but unable to quit without admitting a mistake.
